_comment: Declared mutants. Each entry names one behaviour change and the single test
that must catch it; scripts/check-mutants.py requires the test to pass
Rules for an entry. The mutation must change behaviour, not well-formedness:
neutering a guard so the code below it runs on undefined state makes the
failure a property of the nonsense rather than of the line. It must occur
exactly once in the file. 'why' states the defect the line prevents, so a
reader can judge whether the test is pinning the right thing.
Entries naming a file a branch does not carry are skipped, not failed: each
branch adds the entries for the mechanism it introduces.

mutants.why: An output the node has not buried to the required depth must not be credited, and the disagreement with the indexer must alarm. Without this the exchange credits a deposit a reorganisation can still take back.
A coinbase output is real but unspendable until maturity. Crediting it early hands out a balance the node will refuse to spend, and it is not an indexer disagreement, so it must not alarm either.

An entry is final only when the node has buried the outpoint past MaxReorgDepth. The Ledger contract says Pending may leave out swept outputs, so 'credited and not pending' is not finality: without the depth test a swept credit inside the horizon is recorded final and a reversal after a reorganisation is never re-credited.

A reconcile tick that lands during a backoff must be deferred and made up, not dropped. The full pass is the only safety net against a notification the server never sent, so dropping the tick lets one permanently refused address starve it for the life of the process.

Only two reply timeouts in a row may rebuild the connection. A reply that arrived, even an error, breaks the run; without the reset a timeout, one refused address and another timeout rebuild a healthy connection.

An address that leaves the tracked set must leave the money views with it. The UTXO cache is what GetBalance, GetAllUTXOs and the selector read, so an unpruned entry keeps a retired address's coins spendable.
A listunspent already in flight when TrackAddresses drops its address must not commit, or it undoes the pruning above and makes the output selectable again.

The lying broadcaster must hand the engine a txid that is not the real one. Replacing the first character with a fixed 'f' returns the input unchanged for the one real txid in sixteen that already starts with 'f', and scenario 8 then fails, because it requires a node txid that differs from the engine's own and was handed two that are equal. A spurious failure in one run in sixteen, not a vacuous pass.

Two refreshes of one address can be in flight at once and their replies can arrive in either order. Without the ticket order the older reply commits last, and because the merge drops every output its own reply does not list, a deposit the newer reply found leaves the cache while the record dates the set current.

mutants.replace: if live := c.liveGen.Load(); gen != live && false {
mutants.why: A headers reply buffered on a connection that has since been replaced still answers its caller. Recording its tip moves the height backwards, past the newer one the replacing connection recorded in its handshake.

The pass that follows the first ping timeout has nothing to refresh whenever no address has a change pending. Counted as a clean pass it resets the reply-timeout count, so the second timeout counts as the first and a server that has stopped answering while holding the connection open is never replaced.

mutants.replace: if live := c.liveGen.Load(); gen != live && false {
mutants.why: A subscribe reply from a connection that has been replaced records a status that was true when the server wrote it and dates the address's freshness now, on a connection that carries no subscription for it.

A write that fails on a live context means the socket is gone and dropLocked has forgotten it. Reported as a plain error the refresher classifies it as one the server chose to send, which never rebuilds the connection, and waits out a backoff before finding out through the next call.

Version 2 takes the Argon2id parameters from the file, so a file written with a weak work factor opens as readily as a strong one unless a floor refuses it. Not an edit: editing the parameters changes the derived key and the file stops opening. What is caught is a keystore legitimately created weak, by an older writer or another implementation, whose holder would never learn that its at-rest protection is worth much less than they believe.

The header is plaintext beside the ciphertext and is bound into the AEAD so that an edit to it is a forgery. Every individual field has a second guard, so removing the binding shows up nowhere in the refusals; what is lost is the property itself, that the file authenticates its own header rather than depending on five separate checks all remaining in place.
Version 1 files were sealed with no additional data. Opening one with version 2's bound header makes every keystore written before v0.4 unreadable, which is the loss of the keys in it.

The file records which key source wrote it, and a manager's source is fixed at construction. Without the comparison, a manager holding a Vault key pointed at a passphrase keystore runs Argon2id over an empty passphrase, and the reverse runs HKDF over an empty key; both report a decryption failure and send an operator to look for a wrong passphrase that was never used.

mutants.find: return hkdf.Key(sha256.New, m.extKey, ks.Salt, hkdfInfo, encKeySize)
mutants.replace: return hkdf.Key(sha256.New, m.extKey, nil, hkdfInfo, encKeySize)
mutants.why: An external key does not change between saves. The salt is what makes the AES key differ each time; without it every save of that keystore uses one key, and a 96-bit random nonce carries the whole requirement that no two saves repeat.

The header check runs on the way out as well as on the way in, so this package cannot write a file it would refuse to read. Without that, a writer and a reader that disagree produce a keystore nothing opens, and the disagreement surfaces on the next process start rather than at the save.

The unencrypted public key list is what an operator or an external tool reads to find the address to send to. Version 2 binds it into the AEAD, but version 1 bound nothing, so this comparison against the decrypted records is the only thing that refuses a swapped address in a version 1 file, and a withdrawal goes to whoever edited it.

What the AEAD binds is the canonical re-encoding of the fields this build knows. A field it does not know would be dropped on the way in and never authenticated, so the file would carry content the header's tamper-evidence does not cover.

A json.Decoder reads one value and ignores whatever follows it, where json.Unmarshal refuses it. Without this the refusal of unknown fields covers only the inside of the object, and bytes appended to the file sit outside everything the header's tamper-evidence covers.

Go's decoder keeps the last of two members with the same name, and headerAAD authenticates what the decoder kept. A copy of pubkeys prepended before the real one therefore loads cleanly and is authenticated away, while a reader that takes the first member sees the address the person who edited the file chose.

Save writes the manager's keys over whatever is at the path. Without this test a manager that never read the file replaces the keys in it with its own, which is none on a manager that has only just opened, and returns no error. The keystore is still a keystore afterwards, so nothing downstream reports anything either.

The bit that lets Save overwrite is set where a load succeeds, not where the file is read. A load that got the bytes and then failed to decrypt them knows less about the keystore than one that never opened it, and it is the state an operator retries from. Setting it on the read lets that manager write an empty keystore over a populated one, which is the defect the guard exists for.

The push scenarios believe the fake indexer, so it has to answer every method electrumx.Client sends. A method the client sends and the fake does not answer meets 'unknown method', which the client reads as an error from the server, so a scenario reaching that path takes the error branch and reports success without exercising what it names. A double that has drifted from its client is worse than no double, because it is believed.

mutants.replace: var forwarders = map[string]bool{"Call": true, "call": true, "callGen": true}
mutants.why: The forwarder skip drops a whole function body. Only Call and call forward a method parameter to another caller; callGen and callLocked go to sendLocked and await, so skipping either hides every real call site in its body and the fake can fall behind the client with the coverage test green.
The forwarder skip is keyed on the receiver type as well as the method name. Without the receiver test, any method called call or Call on any type in the package hides every call site in its body.
Every declaration is walked, not only the function declarations: a package-level function literal lives in a GenDecl, and a reading that filters to FuncDecl never sees the call sites inside one.

A client cannot change network once addresses are tracked: the UTXO cache, the subscriptions and every script hash were derived under the old prefix, so it would be asking one network's server about another network's keys and answering 'no coins' for every address.

A write that failed after the rename left the new record in the file. Rolling the map back there makes memory contradict the file, and because every Put writes the whole file from memory the next one puts the older record back over the newer: a Built intent, with a signed transaction and reserved inputs, silently reverts.

The snapshot is the signer's whole view of the chain and it has no other way to check it. An old one lists outputs that may already be spent, so building from it signs a second transaction over inputs the first one used.

The intent id is chosen by the system that asks for the withdrawal and it becomes a file name. Unchecked, a separator or a parent reference writes the record outside the store, or reads another file as a withdrawal.

A save that landed and is only unconfirmed for durability leaves the record in the store, where Recover and any broadcaster will find it Built. Treating that as unsaved releases the inputs of a signed transaction, and the next withdrawal selects them: two transactions stand over one input and one is rejected for good.

A reservation expires by its TTL and is dropped when the set is loaded, and a signer on a new host has no set at all, so a signed withdrawal waiting for the broadcaster can have no reservation in this process. Its inputs are still unspent and therefore in the snapshot, so the pass over the store's Built withdrawals is the only thing keeping the next selection off them.

A case-folding filesystem answers a read of W1.json with w1.json. Without this check the store reports one withdrawal as another, so Submit takes the second as already submitted, its request is moved aside and it is never paid.
